lesson_title: One Captain, or a Rule Book for Everyone?
hook_text: Two teams. In one, the captain can never be questioned. In the other, even the captain must obey the rule book. Which country would you rather live in?
clip_script: Team one. One captain, never elected, never questioned. Only one team allowed in the league. Disagree, and you disappear. Every radio, every newspaper, every film says the captain is a hero. Children march in his youth group. That is fascism. It began with Mussolini in Italy in 1922. Nazi Germany was its most terrible version, with racism at its core, the SS and the secret police arresting people without trial, and neighbours reporting neighbours. Team two. The players vote for their captain, and can vote him out. Anyone can criticise him. A referee he cannot boss around. And a rule book protecting every player, even the captain must obey it. That is democracy. South Africa's rule book is the Constitution of 1996. Its Bill of Rights protects free speech, a free press, equal rights. The Constitutional Court is the referee. One captain. Or a rule book for everyone.
visual_style: Split screen of two teams; on one side a single figure on a podium with loudspeakers and a uniformed youth march; on the other, players voting, a referee's whistle, and a book titled Constitution 1996 glowing.
pacing: Steady build on team one, a beat of silence, an uplifting turn to team two.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson for the features of fascism, life in Nazi Germany and how democracy protects rights.
